items.title: When courts are too slow, police replace judges
items.syllabus: GS2 › Structure, organisation and functioning of the judiciary; Police reforms · GS4 › Probity in governance
items.context: Abhinav Chandrachud argues that years-long civil suits push well-connected litigants to the police, who turn debt and contract disputes into criminal cases of 'cheating' or 'breach of trust'. This creates a parallel, coercive civil-justice system.
ideas: Delay breeds a 'parallel justice' system: police summons and threats of arrest replace a court's verdict.
GS2 judicial pendency, police reforms, access to justice.
The root is too few judges: about 15 per million people in Maharashtra against about 157 in New York state.
GS2 judicial vacancies and infrastructure.
Using criminal law to settle a civil debt is abuse of process; the Supreme Court has discouraged it, but practice lags the law.
GS2 rule of law; GS4 probity and misuse of power.
keywords: Turning debt or contract quarrels into 'cheating' cases
Using legal procedure for an improper aim
Any answer on misuse of police or criminal law.

Law in the books vs law in action

data: Judges per million people: Maharashtra vs New York state
A Bombay HC suit filed in 1947, settled only this year

examples: The Godfather (Puzo, 1969)

pyqs: Free legal aid is not enough if justice takes decades: cite the 79-year Bombay HC suit and ~15 judges per million in Maharashtra against ~157 in New York state.

items.summary: Slow civil courts are pushing creditors to the police, who turn money disputes into criminal cases to force a settlement (Abhinav Chandrachud).
evolution: The Privy Council observed that a litigant's troubles in India begin when he has obtained a decree.

items.context: A former CEA member writes that India has moved from chronic power deficits to a solar-hour glut and night-time deficits. The answer, he argues, is storage, stronger transmission, demand-side management and markets that reward flexibility.
ideas: Capacity is not the goal; power when people need it, by night as well as by day, is.

items.title: Climate justice needs quicker compensation: first Loss and Damage payout to Nepal
items.syllabus: GS3 › Environment; Disaster management · GS2 › International institutions; India's neighbourhood · GS4 › Ethical issues in international funding
items.context: The UN's Fund for Loss and Damage has allocated $21.6 million (about Rs 190 crore) to Nepal, nearly two months after devastating floods. It is the first time the Fund has earmarked a grant for a disaster-affected nation. The Indian Express argues the episode should become a case study for reforming the Fund.
ideas: Loss and damage is compensation, not charity, because it rests on responsibility for climate change.
GS3 climate answers; GS2 global governance.
Speed is justice: delays raise hardship and rebuilding costs, especially for poor countries.
GS3 disaster management; GS4 fairness.
Money is short: $822 million pledged, about a third of pending claims.

items.title: Punjab farm fires: why most stubble-burning incidents are in two districts
items.syllabus: GS3 › Environmental pollution; Cropping patterns; Agricultural technology · GS4 › Ethical dilemmas: private gain vs public good
items.context: Punjab has recorded 684 farm fires this season, 457 of them (69%) in Tarn Taran and Amritsar. Early harvesting of short-duration paddy in the Majha region lets farmers fit in a third crop of peas or potatoes before wheat, which leaves little time to clear fields without burning.
ideas: The real cause is the crop calendar, not just a lack of machines.
GS3 stubble burning and air pollution.
Fires are falling year on year; support and awareness matter as much as penalties.
GS3 policy design; GS4 persuasion over punishment.
Leaving the paddy-wheat cycle is the long-term fix (see Manauli's sweet-corn shift).
GS3 crop diversification.
keywords: Farmers stuck in one crop cycle by MSP and habit
A private act that imposes costs on others
Economics of pollution; GS4 public interest.

data: Farm fires by this point in the season, 2024 → 2025 → 2026
examples: Manauli, Haryana's 'sweet corn village'

pyqs: Majha's third crop and Manauli's shift to sweet corn show diversification in practice.
Why farmers choose high-value crops: Manauli's returns and market links.

items.summary: Most of Punjab's farm fires this season are in Tarn Taran and Amritsar, where a third crop leaves farmers too little time to clear fields without burning.

essay.title: Jogen Chowdhury: refugee to master painter
essay.text: Born into a landed family in Faridpur in pre-Partition East Bengal, he suffered a great reversal of fortune and became a post-Partition refugee in Calcutta. Drawing on memories of the kantha embroidery and alpona floor art of Bengal's village women, he built a personal modern idiom. The tribute calls him a 'hard optimist' and a 'dreamer of institutions'.
essay.use: For 'A thorn is a changed bud', 'Best lessons are learnt through bitter experiences' and 'magical in the mundane' (art from folk floor drawings).

essay.title: Nepal and the first loss-and-damage grant
essay.text: Nepal accounts for barely 0.1% of global emissions, yet floods triggered by an ice-and-rock avalanche claimed more than 1,400 lives and destroyed at least 10% of its hydropower facilities. Developed countries agreed to the grant only after insisting it be treated as an exception, not a precedent.
essay.use: Our suggested link: a contemporary illustration of 'When two elephants fight, it is the grass that gets trampled', and of justice versus charity (compensation, not aid).

essay.title: Lycurgus Cup and Roman concrete: the science in 'magic'
essay.text: A 1,600-year-old Roman cup glows red in normal light and green when lit from behind. Scientists have only now reverse-engineered it. Roman concrete is still not fully recreated, and Indus Valley drainage still has lessons for cities. The editorial argues that the past's real magic is useful achievement, not myths of flying chariots.
essay.use: For 'magical in the mundane', 'The doubter is a true man of science' (versus pseudo-history) and 'Culture is what we are, civilisation is what we have'.

essay.title: The farmer who copied a friend's strawberries
essay.text: In Manauli, Sonipat, Arun Chauhan switched from paddy to sweet corn after visiting a friend's strawberry farm. His village moved 70% of its land to sweet corn and vegetables, formed an FPO and now sells directly to e-commerce firms.
essay.use: For 'The cost of being wrong is less than the cost of doing nothing', 'Ideas with large consequences are simple' and 'A ship in harbour is safe'.

essay.title: Two fathers behind two India cricketers
essay.text: Behind Tilak Varma and Nitish Kumar Reddy, who won a T20I for India in New Zealand, stand two fathers who had hard years. Nitish's father, Mutyala Reddy, left a stable job at Hindustan Zinc Limited to support his son's practice in Visakhapatnam. Tilak's father, Nagaraju, an electrician, spent sleepless nights making ends meet so that his son could concentrate on cricket.
essay.use: For the role of parents and family in shaping a child's future: sacrifice made quietly, years before any success is visible. Fits 'Hand that rocks the cradle rules the world' (the family as the first institution).

essay.title: Angkrish Raghuvanshi's maiden century
essay.text: Out for 92 on debut three years ago, then dropped, the 22-year-old admitted doubting whether he would ever score a first-class hundred. He finally made 114 for Mumbai.
essay.use: For 'Best lessons are learnt through bitter experiences' and 'Ships sink because of water that gets into them' (self-doubt as the real threat).

essay.title: FIDE's first survey of women in chess
essay.text: 76% of 672 female respondents from 127 federations reported discrimination or harassment. 44% considered stepping away from chess, and 54% never had a female role model or mentor. India was the largest contributor, with 69 respondents.
essay.use: Fresh data for gender-justice essays ('Patriarchy is the least noticed yet most significant structure...'). The lack of mentors shows 'restrictions' at work.

essay.title: From 'use and throw' to 'use, return and recover'
essay.text: Delhi's planned bottle-deposit scheme. Uttarakhand's version raised bottle return rates from about 20% to nearly 90% with a refundable Rs 10 deposit.
essay.use: For nature and ethics essays: small nudges, big behaviour change ('Ideas with large consequences are simple').

essay.title: Ageing with dignity: Keralam's elder-rights law
essay.text: Keralam's new law gives senior citizens the right to age at home, recognises living wills, and regulates care homes and caregivers. The Chief Minister called it a realisation that 'our world is changing'.
essay.use: For 'Life is a long journey between human being and being humane', 'The years teach much...' and 'Hand that rocks the cradle' (care work).
